claim: The organizer (the tip of the primitive streak, Hensen's node) can redirect the fate of non-neural ectoderm cells to form a complete, patterned nervous system.
source: During early vertebrate development, signals from a special region of the embryo, the organizer, can redirect the fate of non-neural ectoderm cells to form a complete, patterned nervous system.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon, supported by the experimental design described throughout the paper.

claim: The responding ectoderm requires about 12 hr of exposure to the organizer to acquire neural identity in a stable way ('commitment').
source: But it is clear from timed grafting and subsequent removal of organizer transplants that the responding ectoderm requires about 12 hr of exposure to the organizer to acquire neural identity in a stable way ('commitment') (Gallera and Ivanov, 1964; Gallera, 1971b; Streit et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and is consistent with the experimental design of the current study.

claim: OTX2 is first expressed in the pre-primitive-streak stage epiblast at EGKXII-XIII.
source: OTX2 is first expressed in the pre-primitive-streak stage epiblast at EGKXII-XIII (Albazerchi and Stern, 2007; Pinho et al., 2011) and is induced by 7/7 grafts after 3 hr (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SOX2 is first expressed at HH4+/5 and requires 9 hr for induction by a node graft.
source: SOX2 is first expressed at HH4+/5 (Rex et al., 1997; Streit et al., 1997; Streit et al., 1998; Sheng et al., 2003) and requires 9 hr for induction (8/8) (Figure 1G–K).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SOX1 starts to be expressed weakly in the neural plate around HH7-8 and is induced by 50% of grafts after 12 hr.
source: SOX1 starts to be expressed weakly in the neural plate around HH7-8 (Stavridis et al., 2010; Uchikawa et al., 2011) and is induced by 50% of grafts after 12 hr (Figure 1L–P).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RNAseq analysis identified 8673 differentially expressed transcripts in response to node grafts at 5, 9, or 12 hr.
source: When 'induced' and 'uninduced' reads at each time point are compared by DESeq analyses, 8673 differentially expressed transcripts were identified (see volcano plots, Figure 1R–T).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by the volcano plots in Figure 1R-T.

claim: Of the 8673 differentially expressed transcripts, 4130 were upregulated and 4543 were downregulated in induced tissue relative to uninduced tissue.
source: Of these, 4130 were upregulated (enriched in 'induced' tissue) and 4543 were downregulated (depleted in 'induced' tissue) relative to the 'uninduced' counterpart.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text as a result of the DESeq analysis.

claim: 482 transcription factors and chromatin modifiers are differentially expressed during neural induction.
source: To construct a GRN we focused on 482 transcription factors and chromatin modifiers that are differentially expressed within these data.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1U.

claim: Of the 482 transcriptional regulators, 255 are upregulated, 203 are downregulated, and 24 have more complex expression dynamics.
source: Of these 'transcriptional regulators', 255 are upregulated, 203 are downregulated, and 24 have more complex expression dynamics (Figure 1U and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1U and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H3K27ac is associated with actively transcribed genes and their enhancers.
source: For example, H3K27ac is associated with actively transcribed genes and their enhancers, whereas transcriptionally inactive regions are often marked by H3K27me3 (Tiwari et al., 2008; Heintzman et al., 2009; Creyghton et al., 2010; Kharchenko et al., 2011; Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011; Tolhuis et al., 2011; Zentner et al., 2011; Bonn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: H3K27me3 marks transcriptionally inactive regions.
source: For example, H3K27ac is associated with actively transcribed genes and their enhancers, whereas transcriptionally inactive regions are often marked by H3K27me3 (Tiwari et al., 2008; Heintzman et al., 2009; Creyghton et al., 2010; Kharchenko et al., 2011; Rada-Iglesias et al., 2011; Tolhuis et al., 2011; Zentner et al., 2011; Bonn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: As neural induction progresses, the number of chromatin sites undergoing activation increases.
source: Overall, as neural induction progresses, the number of sites undergoing activation increases, along with a reduction in those that do not change state.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation from the ChIPseq data analysis.

claim: There is little difference in chromatin accessibility between induced and uninduced samples at 5 hr, but differences become more marked at later time points.
source: In contrast, ATACseq suggests that there is little difference between induced and uninduced samples in terms of chromatin accessibility (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) at 5 hr, but the differences become more marked at later time points.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 12 hr, the ATACseq profile of induced tissue resembles that of the endogenous neural plate of the embryo.
source: At 12 hr, the ATACseq profile resembles that of the endogenous neural plate of the embryo (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The gene regulatory network comprises 175 transcriptional regulators and 5614 predicted interactions between them.
source: The resulting GRN (Figure 4C), depicting interactions between 175 genes, was represented using BioTapestry (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In total, 5614 interactions are predicted to occur between the 175 GRN components.
source: In total, 5614 interactions are predicted to occur between these components, highlighting the intricate and highly dynamic sequence of regulatory events that are triggered by signals from the organizer.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text as a result of the GRN analysis.

claim: The pre-streak epiblast is most similar to induced ectoderm after 5 hr of a node graft.
source: When these embryonic tissues (Figure 7A) are compared to neural induction, we find that the pre-streak epiblast is most similar to induced ectoderm after 5 hr of a node graft, while 9 and 12 hr time points are more closely related to mature neural plate (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 9 and 12 hr time points after node graft are more closely related to mature neural plate.
source: When these embryonic tissues (Figure 7A) are compared to neural induction, we find that the pre-streak epiblast is most similar to induced ectoderm after 5 hr of a node graft, while 9 and 12 hr time points are more closely related to mature neural plate (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 84 out of 89 transcriptional regulators that are induced by a node graft were detected in neural tissues at some stage.
source: In total, 84/89 transcriptional regulators that are induced by a node graft were detected in neural tissues at some stage (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7 and supplements.

claim: Most of the transcriptional regulators that are induced by a node graft (79/84) have not previously been associated with neural induction.
source: Most of the transcriptional regulators that are induced by a node graft (79/84) have not previously been associated with neural induction (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the source data.

claim: A high proportion (65/85; 76%) of the transcripts that are downregulated after a node graft are depleted in neural tissues relative to non-neural territories.
source: Likewise, a high proportion (65/85; 76%) of the transcripts that are downregulated after a node graft are depleted in neural tissues relative to non-neural territories.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a result of the in situ hybridization analysis.

claim: GRN components upregulated within 1–5 hr of a node graft are initially highly expressed in prospective neural cells and their expression decreases progressively across PC1.
source: This analysis reveals that components upregulated within 1–5 hr of a node graft are initially highly expressed in prospective neural cells and that their expression decreases progressively across PC1.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a result of the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: GRN components that are induced after 7–12 hr are expressed at higher levels later, in cells of the maturing neural plate and neural tube.
source: GRN components that are induced after 7–12 hr are expressed at higher levels later, in cells of the maturing neural plate and neural tube.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a result of the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: GRN components identified from node graft experiments are expressed in a temporal hierarchy that closely replicates normal neural plate development.
source: Therefore, GRN components identified from node graft experiments are expressed in a temporal hierarchy that closely replicates normal neural plate development.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the scRNAseq analysis.

claim: Each of the six tested enhancers drives neural-specific GFP expression in a spatiotemporal pattern strikingly similar to the gene that lies in its proximity.
source: Each enhancer drives neural-specific GFP expression in a spatiotemporal pattern strikingly similar to the gene that lies in its proximity (Figure 9B–O and Figure 9—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the reporter assay data shown in Figure 9 and supplements.

claim: The domain of reporter activity for all six predicted enhancers corresponds to that of the normal expression of the associated gene.
source: Therefore, the domain of reporter activity for all six predicted enhancers corresponds to that of the normal expression of the associated gene.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the reporter assay experiments.

claim: The stage at which the reporter first becomes active closely matches the stage at which the gene starts to be expressed during normal development.
source: Furthermore, the stage at which the reporter first becomes active closely matches the stage at which the gene starts to be expressed during normal development.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the reporter assay experiments.

claim: Electroporation of a morpholino against MYCN knocks down the expression of ZNF423.
source: Electroporation of a morpholino against MYCN into the prospective neural plate at HH3/3+ (Figure 9Q) knocks down the expression of ZNF423 (Figure 9R–S; 5/10 embryos), which is usually expressed later in the neural plate and neural tube (Figure 7J), compared to a control morpholino (Figure 9T–U; 1/10 embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Histone profiles that change in response to a node graft can predict regulatory elements relevant to neural development.
source: Taken together, these comparisons between node grafts and normal embryos strongly suggest that histone profiles that change in response to a node graft (upon which our network is based) can predict regulatory elements relevant to neural development.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the combined analyses.

claim: The hierarchy of responses to a graft of Hensen's node into a remote part of the embryo closely recapitulates the events of normal neural plate development.
source: We show that the hierarchy of responses to a graft of Hensen's node into a remote part of the embryo closely recapitulates the events of normal neural plate development, including not only the timing of gene expression in the developing neural plate, but also appropriate spatiotemporal activity of enhancers identified by the graft assay.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The GRN represents the most comprehensive example to date of a detailed network in a vertebrate embryo, modelled on both transcriptional and chromatin changes that take place in vivo, at high temporal resolution.
source: This represents the most comprehensive example to date of a detailed network in a vertebrate embryo, modelled on both transcriptional and chromatin changes that take place in vivo, at high temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a claim about the significance of the study.

claim: Grafting an organizer to a region of ectoderm that does not normally contribute to neural tissue provides the opportunity to study the progress of neural induction relative to 'time-zero'.
source: Grafting an organizer to a region of ectoderm that does not normally contribute to neural tissue (but is competent to do so) provides the opportunity to study the progress of neural induction relative to 'time-zero', the moment when the organizer is first presented to the tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: Sites that are remote enough from the normal neural plate and are competent to respond to an organizer graft can generate a complete neural tube without induction of mesoderm, and without recruiting cells from the host's neural plate.
source: It also allows for the separation of neural inductive events from other processes that occur adjacent to the normal neural plate (e.g. mesendoderm formation and patterning), because sites that are remote enough from the normal neural plate and are competent to respond to an organizer graft can generate a complete neural tube without induction of mesoderm, and without recruiting cells from the host's neural plate (Hornbruch et al., 1979; Dias and Schoenwolf, 1990; Storey et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: A graft of Hensen's node to the inner area opaca induces the formation of a mature, patterned neural tube after about 15 hr of culture.
source: In the chick embryo, a graft of Hensen's node to the inner area opaca, an extraembryonic region of competent non-neural ectoderm (Gallera and Ivanov, 1964; Dias and Schoenwolf, 1990; Storey et al., 1992; Streit et al., 1998), induces the formation of a mature, patterned neural tube after about 15 hr of culture from the host ectoderm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by Figure 1A and citations.

claim: The inner area opaca is an extraembryonic region of competent non-neural ectoderm.
source: In the chick embryo, a graft of Hensen's node to the inner area opaca, an extraembryonic region of competent non-neural ectoderm (Gallera and Ivanov, 1964; Dias and Schoenwolf, 1990; Storey et al., 1992; Streit et al., 1998), induces the formation of a mature, patterned neural tube after about 15 hr of culture from the host ectoderm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by citations.

claim: The organizer was discovered 100 years ago by Spemann and Mangold.
source: One of the most influential studies in developmental biology was the discovery, 100 years ago, that a small region of the vertebrate embryo, named the 'organizer', can induce ectodermal cells that do not normally contribute to the neural plate to form a complete, patterned nervous system (Spemann, 1921; Spemann and Mangold, 1924).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In amphibians, the 'organizer' resides in the dorsal lip of the blastopore.
source: In amphibians, where these experiments were initially conducted, the 'organizer' resides in the dorsal lip of the blastopore.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: In birds and mammals, the organizer is the tip of the primitive streak, known as Hensen's node.
source: A few years later, Waddington demonstrated that an equivalent region exists in birds (duck and chick) and mammals (rabbit) (Waddington, 1933; Waddington and Schmidt, 1933; Waddington, 1934; Waddington, 1936; Waddington, 1937): the tip of the primitive streak, a structure known as Hensen's node (Hensen, 1876).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between the organizer and the responding ectoderm has been termed 'neural induction'.
source: This interaction between the organizer and the responding ectoderm, which causes the latter to acquire neural plate identity, has been termed 'neural induction' (Spemann and Mangold, 1924; Nieuwkoop, 1952; Gallera, 1971b; Saxén, 1980; Gurdon, 1987; Storey et al., 1992; Stern, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Neural induction has often been imagined as a single event, 'switching' the fate of the responding tissue from non-neural to neural.
source: Neural induction has often been imagined as a single event, 'switching' the fate of the responding tissue from non-neural to neural.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a common historical view.

claim: The expression of many genes changes over time after grafting an organizer, suggesting that the process has considerable complexity.
source: Recent work has also revealed that the expression of many genes changes over time after grafting an organizer, suggesting that the process has considerable complexity (Streit et al., 1997; Streit et al., 1998; Streit and Stern, 1999; Streit et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 2003; Stern, 2005; Albazerchi and Stern, 2007; Papanayotou et al., 2008; Gibson et al., 2011; Pinho et al., 2011; Papanayotou et al., 2013; Trevers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Competent ectoderm cannot respond to BMP inhibitors like Chordin unless it has previously been exposed to a graft of the organizer for at least 5 hr.
source: Functional studies have established that competent ectoderm cannot respond to BMP inhibitors like Chordin unless it has previously been exposed to a graft of the organizer for at least 5 hr (Streit et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: BLIMP1 (PRDX1) is required transiently at an early stage for neural plate, crest, and placode development, and its subsequent downregulation is also essential for further differentiation.
source: Indeed, BLMP1 (PRDX1) has recently been shown to be required transiently at an early stage for neural plate, crest, and placode development, and its subsequent downregulation is also essential for further differentiation (Prajapati et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: In the normal embryo, it is the hypoblast rather than the node that initiates the 'common state' associated with early neural induction.
source: This suggests that in the normal embryo, it is the hypoblast rather than the node that initiates this process (Foley et al., 2000; Streit et al., 2000; Trevers et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: A large part of the prospective CNS (forebrain, midbrain, and anterior hindbrain) is never close to the node but extends far anteriorly from the primitive streak.
source: For these reasons, the time course initiated by a transplanted tissue that is able to induce a complete nervous system in a responding tissue whose fate is not to form a neural plate is an invaluable tool to study the acquisition of neural plate identity. Here, we have taken advantage of this approach by first constructing a GRN with a fine time course in a competent responding tissue after such a transplant, defining the hierarchy and dynamics of expression of more than 150 transcription factors and other markers, along with changes in chromatin marks that accompany this. Then, we addressed the question of whether this hierarchy of events is in any way comparable to what occurs during normal neural development, using three complementary approaches:
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation about normal development.

claim: The most anterior nervous system may be induced by signals other than the node, as well as earlier in development.
source: Indeed it has been suggested that the most anterior nervous system may be induced by signals other than the node, as well as earlier in development, and that the node and its derivatives may be involved mainly in the induction of the more caudal parts of the CNS (posterior hindbrain and spinal cord) (Beddington, 1994; Thomas and Beddington, 1996; Foley et al., 2000; Streit et al., 2000; Metzis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Out of 84 upregulated genes included in the network, the majority (74/84) are expressed in the prospective mouse neural plate.
source: Indeed, we have noticed that out of 84 upregulated genes included in this network, the majority (74/84) are expressed in the prospective mouse neural plate (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by source data.

claim: These 84 genes include 69 not previously associated with neural induction in any species, of which the majority (56/69) are expressed in the future mouse neural plate.
source: These 84 genes include 69 not previously associated with neural induction in any species, of which the majority (56/69) are expressed in the future mouse neural plate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by source data.

claim: The observations suggest a high degree of evolutionary conservation of neural induction mechanisms.
source: These observations suggest a high degree of evolutionary conservation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data.
